title: Is Chevron a Buy, Sell, or Hold at $110 Oil? - The Globe and Mail
content: Chevron has one of the lowest-cost operations in the oil patch. The company can make a lot of money as oil prices rise. Oil prices have risen sharply due to the war with Iran. Brent oil, the global benchmark, recently traded above $110 a barrel amid continued supply disruptions in the Middle East. The price of Brent has surged nearly 90% this year. Here is a look at whether investors should buy, sell, or hold Chevron(NYSE: CVX) stock, given the current price of crude oil. Will AI create the world's first trillionaire? Our team just released a report on the one little-known company, called an "Indispensable Monopoly" providing the critical technology Nvidia and Intel both need. Continue » Chevron is one of the largest and lowest-cost producers in the oil sector. The company can generate enough cash to cover its capital program and dividend at less than $50 a barrel through 2030. With crude prices currently double that level, Chevron is producing significant surplus free cash flow. The company initially estimated that it would produce an incremental $12.5 billion in free cash flow this year if oil averaged $70 a barrel, fueled by recently completed expansion projects, its acquisition of Hess, and cost-savings initiatives. It should generate significantly more free cash flow this year if oil prices remain elevated. However, the company isn't yet experiencing the full impact of higher prices. During the first quarter, Chevron's profits fell despite higher oil prices and production. That was due to timing mismatches related to financial derivatives on products it hasn't yet delivered. Its earnings and cash flow will improve as it delivers those products in the future, assuming oil prices remain elevated. Chevron estimates that every $1 increase in the average annual price of Brent crude will boost its full-year cash flow by $600 million. While oil prices have soared during the first half of this year, there's a lot of uncertainty about where they will be in the second half. There's currently a stalemate in peace talks between the U.S. and Iran, which is prolonging the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The longer it remains closed, the higher oil prices could go. For example, JPMorgan recently warned that Brent could spike to the $120-$130 a barrel range in the near term, with the risk of surging to about $150 if the Strait remains disrupted through mid-May. Under this scenario, oil would remain above $100 a barrel in the second quarter before declining in the second half as oil flows normalize and inventory levels rebuild. Goldman Sachs also recently raised its oil price forecast for this year. Its base case is that Brent will average $90 a barrel in the fourth quarter. That's due to its expectation that oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz won't normalize until the end of June. Meanwhile, a more adverse case projects that oil could remain above $100 through the rest of the year. While most forecasters now expect that oil prices will remain high for the rest of the year, they anticipate lower prices in 2027 and beyond. For example, the U.S. Energy Information Administration's latest short-term energy outlook estimates that Brent will average $96 in 2026 and $76 next year. Oil could head even lower in the coming years as the UAE ramps up production now that it has left OPEC. While oil prices have soared this year, Chevron's stock has risen more modestly at about 25%. Investors seem to be pricing in a quick recovery of oil supplies once the Strait of Hormuz reopens, and a more rapid descent in crude prices later this year. While that's entirely possible, there's meaningful upside risk to crude prices if the war reignites and the Strait remains closed. Meanwhile, even if the current market expectations play out, Chevron can still thrive at lower oil prices. It expects to grow its free cash flow at a more than 10% annual rate through 2030 at $70 oil, while fully funding its capital spending and dividend at sub-$50 oil. Chevron's upside potential to higher prices and ability to thrive if they fall make the oil stock a buy at $110 oil. Economies will need to adjust demand due to reduced supply, with contraction expected to first appear in Asia.He noted that commercial market inventories, sanction-evading shadow fleets and strategic reserves of various countries are being gradually depleted. Demand must adjust to adapt to reduced supply, and economic growth will inevitably have to slow. Asia is most dependent on Persian Gulf crude oil and refineries, with Europe likely to be affected subsequently. He specifically pointed out that the last scheduled shipments of oil from the Persian Gulf are currently being unloaded at the Port of Long Beach in California.He believes the scale of the impact from the Strait of Hormuz blockade could be comparable to the oil crisis of the 1970s. content: Villere St Denis J & Co LLC Exited position in Euronet WorldWide 244,878 shares, estimated transaction value of $17.53 million based on quarterly average pricing Quarter-end position value decreased by $18.64 million, reflecting both sale activity and price movement Change represents 1.93% of 13F reportable assets under management The position previously accounted for 1.9% of the fund’s AUM as of the prior quarter; this marks a full liquidation According to a filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission dated April 30, 2026, Villere St Denis J & Co LLC sold all 244,878 shares of Euronet Worldwide(NASDAQ:EEFT)during the first quarter. The fund’s quarter-end position value in the company declined by $18.64 million, reflecting the combined effect of share sales and market price changes. Villere St Denis J & Co LLC fully exited its Euronet Worldwide position, which previously made up 1.9% of 13F assets under management; the post-sale allocation is now n/a As of April 29, 2026, Euronet Worldwide shares were priced at $75.33, down 25.4% over the past year, underperforming the S&P 500 by 53.69 percentage points Euronet Worldwide operates a global payments infrastructure, managing over 42,000 ATMs and hundreds of thousands of POS terminals across multiple regions. Its diversified business model spans electronic fund transfers, prepaid product distribution, and money transfer services, enabling the company to capture transaction fees from both institutional and retail clients. The company generates revenue through transaction-based fees from its ATM/POS networks, payment processing, and money transfer services, supported by extensive global infrastructure and technology platforms. Euronet's scale, technology assets, and broad customer base support its position as a leading provider of electronic payment and money movement solutions worldwide. Its primary customers include financial institutions, retailers, merchants, agents, content providers, and individual consumers worldwide. Euronet Worldwide operates as a global money-movement company with three main business lines: electronic funds transfer, prepaid and digital distribution, and money transfer. This structure makes the stock more complex than a typical payments network, since ATM activity, merchant acquiring, retailer distribution, and foreign exchange all influence results in different ways. The key question for Euronet is whether transaction growth is leading to higher profits across these areas. Electronic funds transfers gain from ATM activity, merchant acquiring, infrastructure services, and banking partnerships. Money Transfer depends on the health of specific remittance corridors, where volume growth, pricing, and digital adoption do not always move together. Epay adds a different layer through prepaid and digital distribution, which is tied more closely to retailer networks and consumer payment behavior. Together, those businesses give Euronet more than one path to growth, but they also make profitability sensitive to regional demand, currency swings, and compliance costs. For investors, Euronet is less about a single payments theme and more about whether its transaction networks can deliver consistent earnings across regions and product lines. The opportunity is that scale and cross-border activity can support growth if volumes translate into better margins. The risk is that pressure in one part of the business, such as money transfer pricing or weaker regional demand, can offset gains elsewhere, thus making results harder to read than those of simpler payment-network companies. title: Chevron (CVX) Q1 2026: Adj EPS of $1.41; Hess Integration Drives 15% Production Surge - AlphaStreet
content: Chevron Corporation delivered a sharp contrast between reported and adjusted results in Q1 2026: GAAP net income fell to $2.2 billion ($1.11 per diluted share) — the company’s lowest quarterly profit in five years — yet adjusted (non-GAAP) EPS of $1.41 crushed analyst consensus of approximately $0.97 by 45%. The disconnect reflects downstream timing charges and lower crude realizations versus Q1 2025, while the underlying operational story was one of production expansion. Net oil-equivalent production averaged 3.86 million barrels of oil equivalent per day (BOE/day), up approximately 15% year-over-year, driven by the integration of Hess Corporation assets acquired in 2025. Chevron’s Q1 2026 GAAP net income of $2.2 billion ($1.11/share) compared to $3.5 billion ($2.00/share) in Q1 2025 — a 37% decline in reported profit. However, this figure includes downstream timing charges and lower crude price realizations driven by the Iran-Middle East conflict environment, which depressed oil sales prices relative to what derivative hedges had priced in. Adjusted (non-GAAP) earnings of $2.8 billion translate to $1.41 per share — a figure that strips out the non-cash timing charges and one-time items. Against analyst consensus of approximately $0.97, the $1.41 adj EPS represents a 45% beat. The divergence is the defining feature of this quarter. The revenue figure of approximately $48.6 billion was roughly in line with expectations despite a large miss vs. some estimates — the variance reflects realized oil and gas prices that lagged headline crude benchmarks due to timing of sales and hedging positions. The operational highlight of Q1 2026 was production volume. Net oil-equivalent production of 3.86 million BOE/day is up approximately 15% year-over-year, reflecting the first full production contribution quarter from Hess assets following the acquisition completed in mid-2025. Key production drivers include the Gulf of Mexico / Guyana fields inherited from Hess, continued Permian Basin growth, and Tengizchevroil (TCO) in Kazakhstan. This volume growth is strategically significant: even as crude oil prices were volatile due to the Iran war dynamic, Chevron was producing substantially more barrels than a year earlier. If pricing normalizes, the volume increase directly multiplies into earnings. Chevron maintained its FY2026 production guidance of 7% to 10% growth versus 2025 levels (at $60 Brent, excluding asset sale impacts) and an organic capex range of $18–$19 billion. The GAAP profit decline to $2.2 billion was driven primarily by three factors: Adjusted earnings of $2.8 billion remove these distortions and show a business that, despite lower realized prices, was generating substantial earnings on the back of a 15% production increase. Chevron’s capital framework remains consistent: organic capex guidance of $18–$19 billion for FY2026 is unchanged, and the company targets 7%–10% production growth vs. 2025. With the Hess integration largely complete, incremental production growth in future quarters will be driven by organic activity rather than integration step-ups. title: Chevron Earnings Call Balances Headwinds With Growth - The Globe and Mail
content: Chevron ((CVX)) has held its Q1 earnings call. Read on for the main highlights of the call. Chevron’s latest earnings call struck a broadly constructive tone despite several sizable one‑off and timing headwinds that weighed on reported results. Management stressed strong operations, robust cash generation, and rising production, while reiterating capital discipline, buybacks, and dividend growth, signaling confidence in the company’s long‑term value story. Chevron reported first‑quarter earnings of $2.2 billion, or $1.11 per share, alongside adjusted earnings of $2.8 billion, or $1.41 per share, once legal and FX impacts are stripped out. The spread between GAAP and adjusted results highlighted underlying profitability even as reported EPS absorbed a $360 million legal reserve and foreign‑exchange pressure. Cash flow from operations excluding working capital reached $7.1 billion, reflecting resilient underlying cash generation despite volatile markets. Adjusted free cash flow came in at $4.1 billion, boosted by a $1 billion loan repayment from the TCO project, supporting continued shareholder returns and balance‑sheet strength. Oil‑equivalent production climbed by about 500,000 barrels per day year over year, underlining Chevron’s growth momentum. U.S. volumes exceeded 2.0 million boe per day, with the Permian and TCO each producing above 1.0 million boe per day, reinforcing the company’s scale and leverage to upstream volumes. Gorgon and Wheatstone LNG assets ran at full rates, contributing to a roughly 16 million ton per year LNG portfolio that management plans to expand to about 20 million tons by 2030. Executives emphasized strong upstream fundamentals and peer‑leading cash margins, positioning LNG as a key long‑term earnings and cash engine. U.S. refineries operated at record crude throughput levels, and Chevron highlighted rising equity crude runs as a strategic advantage. Equity crude throughput is expected to more than double year over year to about 40% in the second quarter, with global optimization across upstream and downstream helping to maximize realized margins. Organic capital spending totaled $3.9 billion in the quarter, with management reaffirming the full‑year capital budget of $18–19 billion. Chevron repurchased $2.5 billion of shares, consistent with its $2.5–3.0 billion quarterly buyback framework, underscoring a continued commitment to capital returns. Management kept 2026 guidance unchanged and reiterated expected production growth of 7–10% for this year, despite near‑term volatility. The company remains on track for $3–4 billion in structural cost reductions by year‑end and reiterated 2030 goals of more than 10% growth in adjusted free cash flow and EPS plus about a 3% ROCE uplift at $70 Brent. Chevron expects Venezuela to contribute roughly 1–2% of cash flow from operations as receivable recovery improves over the next several years. Equity affiliate distributions guidance was raised by more than $2 billion versus the first quarter run‑rate, and TCO has shifted to monthly dividends, supporting more regular cash inflows. Earnings were hit by around $3.0 billion of unfavorable timing effects tied to a sharp commodity price spike in March, split between inventory valuation and derivative mark‑to‑market. Management expects about $1.0 billion of these paper positions to reverse in the second quarter, suggesting some relief as prices normalize. Adjusted earnings fell by $440 million compared with the prior quarter, driven mainly by weaker downstream performance. The decline was largely tied to timing and inventory effects, partly offset by firmer refining margins, indicating that core demand and margin trends remain more resilient than the headline drop. The quarter included a $360 million legal reserve that reduced reported profits, reminding investors of ongoing legal risks that occasionally surface in large portfolios. Foreign‑exchange moves shaved another $223 million from earnings, an external factor that management framed as transitory rather than structural. Sharp commodity price increases and inventory builds drove a working capital outflow, masking the strength of operating cash flow. Chevron issued more than $5 billion in commercial paper to bridge short‑term liquidity needs and had repaid about half by April, signaling confidence in near‑term cash recovery. Downstream results were negatively affected by mark‑to‑market losses on physical‑linked derivatives and inventory timing in a rapidly moving price environment. Management acknowledged that this exposure can swing quarterly results but stressed that these impacts are largely non‑cash and tend to normalize over time. While operations and receivable recovery in Venezuela are improving, management highlighted ongoing uncertainties around taxes, royalties, and dispute mechanisms. These unresolved fiscal and contractual terms limit the company’s willingness to deploy additional capital there, keeping Venezuela as an option rather than a core growth pillar. Chevron reaffirmed its full‑year capital budget, multi‑year production growth targets, and structural cost‑cutting plans, signaling no change to its strategic roadmap. With stronger volumes, expanding LNG, and rising equity crude throughput, management expects adjusted free cash flow and earnings to grow meaningfully toward 2030, even at moderate oil prices. The earnings call painted a picture of a company absorbing sizable short‑term hits while delivering solid operations and sticking to its capital return promises. For investors, the key takeaway is that Chevron’s long‑term growth, efficiency gains, and shareholder‑friendly policies remain intact despite a noisy quarter dominated by timing, legal, and FX headwinds.
